content.content:
# Postmark — transactional email for Next.js Postmark sends an app's transactional email (welcome emails, password resets, receipts) with high delivery rates, bounce and spam processing, and detailed statistics. The official Node.js library `postmark` covers the whole Postmark REST API, uses the native Fetch API and has no runtime dependencies (Node 18+). ## Install ```bash npm install postmark ``` ## 1. Environment variables `.env.local`: ``` POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN=server_token_placeholder POSTMARK_FROM_EMAIL=hello@example.com ``` The server token belongs to one Postmark server (Servers → API Tokens). The From address must be a confirmed sender signature or sit on a verified domain. ## 2. Create a client `src/lib/postmark.ts`: ```ts import { ServerClient } from "postmark"; export const postmark = new ServerClient(process.env.POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN!); ``` Use the client only in server code (route handlers, server actions, server components). Never expose the server token to the browser. ## 3. Send an email ```ts import { postmark } from "@/lib/postmark"; await postmark.sendEmail({ From: process.env.POSTMARK_FROM_EMAIL!, To: "user@example.com", Subject: "Welcome!", HtmlBody: "

Thanks for signing up.

", TextBody: "Thanks for signing up.", MessageStream: "outbound", }); ``` `outbound` is the default transactional message stream. Keep transactional and broadcast email in separate streams. ## 4. Send with a template Create the template once in the Postmark dashboard, then send it by alias: ```ts await postmark.sendEmailWithTemplate({ From: process.env.POSTMARK_FROM_EMAIL!, To: "user@example.com", TemplateAlias: "password-reset", TemplateModel: { name: "Ada", action_url: "https://example.com/reset?token=..." }, MessageStream: "outbound", }); ``` `TemplateId` (a number) works in place of `TemplateAlias`. ## 5. Handle errors `sendEmail` returns a promise that rejects with a typed error from `postmark`'s `Errors` export when Postmark refuses the message (inactive recipient, unconfirmed sender, invalid token). Catch it where the email is triggered so a failed email does not break the request that caused it. ## Why teams pick Postmark - Built for transactional email: high delivery rates, with bounce and spam handling included. - Templates live in the dashboard, so copy changes do not need a deploy. - Detailed delivery statistics and inbound email parsing come with the same account. # env files (can opt-in for committing if needed) .env* next-env.d.ts # Notely A small team notes app. Next.js App Router + TypeScript + Tailwind. ## Status - Users live in `src/lib/users.ts` as an in-memory list. - `/dashboard` shows the current user and the team. - There is no sign-in, no billing, and no email yet. ## Develop ```bash npm run dev ```

content.text:
Notely now sends a welcome email when a user is created and a password reset email, both through **Postmark**. The build, typecheck and lint all pass. I tested the whole flow with Postmark's API stubbed out, so no real email has been sent yet.

**Why Postmark:** it only does transactional email, delivers reliably, and handles bounces and spam complaints for you. Its official Node package (`postmark`, published by ActiveCampaign) has no other dependencies. The project already had a Postmark quickstart in `docs/`, so I followed that.

**What changed**
- **`src/lib/postmark.ts`**: sets up the Postmark connection. It only starts on the first send, so the app builds and runs without a token.
- **`src/lib/email.ts`**: `sendWelcomeEmail` and `sendPasswordResetEmail`. The email text (HTML and plain-text versions) lives in the code, so nothing needs setting up in the Postmark dashboard. User names are escaped before going into the HTML. If a send fails, the error is logged and the function returns `false` instead of crashing, so a bounced email can't break sign-up.
- **`src/lib/users.ts`**:
  - `createUser` checks the email and name, rejects duplicate emails, and sends the welcome email.
  - `requestPasswordReset(email)` creates a random single-use link that expires after 60 minutes and emails it. It returns the same thing whether or not the email exists, so nobody can use it to find out who has an account. Only a hash of each token is stored.
  - `resetPassword(token, newPassword)` checks the token and saves the new password, hashed with scrypt.
  - Also added: `getUserByEmail` and `verifyPassword`. Password hashes are stored separately from `User`, so `listUsers` never exposes them.
- **`src/app/reset-password/page.tsx`**: a small page so the link in the email actually works. It has a "send reset link" form and a "set new password" form.
- **`.env.example`**: `POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN`, `POSTMARK_FROM_EMAIL` and `APP_URL`, with placeholder values. I added `!.env.example` to `.gitignore` because the existing `.env*` rule would have hidden it.
- Installed `postmark` and `server-only`, and updated the README.

**What the stubbed test showed:** a welcome email goes out on `createUser`. A rejected recipient doesn't crash it. An unknown email gets no reset email. A reset link works once, and a used or fake one is rejected. The new password checks out afterwards.

**Before it sends real email**
- Put a real server token in `.env.local`. The From address has to be a confirmed sender or on a verified domain in Postmark.
- Users are still stored in memory, and that now includes passwords and reset tokens, so they all disappear on restart. That's fine until there's a database.
- `verifyPassword` is there, but nothing uses it yet because the app has no sign-in.

I haven't committed anything.
